summary: Learners aged 11–12 investigate how a single-celled organism (such as Amoeba, Euglena or Paramecium) carries out ALL seven life processes (movement, respiration, sensitivity, nutrition, excretion, reproduction, growth — MRS GREN/MRS NERG) within its one cell, using structural adaptations instead of specialised organs. The central insight: one cell is a complete, self-sufficient life, and its adaptations substitute for the organs a multicellular body uses. Each adaptation belongs to a specific organism (pseudopod — Amoeba; flagellum + eyespot — Euglena; cilia — Paramecium; contractile vacuole — all three), so no single microbe should be shown with all of them at once. Work should start concrete (a single named microbe, one process at a time), contrast unicellular self-sufficiency with multicellular division of labour, and deliberately challenge the 'all microbes are germs' misconception.
misconceptions: Believing all single-celled organisms are harmful 'germs' — most are harmless or beneficial.
Thinking a single cell is too simple to be fully alive / cannot do all life processes — in fact it does every one.
Confusing bacteria (prokaryotic, no nucleus) with Amoeba/Euglena (eukaryotic protists) as if all microbes are the same kind of cell.
Assuming unicellular organisms don't move or respond to their surroundings.
Thinking multicellular organisms are just 'bigger versions' of single cells rather than having specialised cells for different jobs.

activities.title: Keep the single cell alive: pilot one microbe through every life process
steps: Take control of one named microbe in a model environment and keep it alive over time; the adaptations shown should match the organism you choose, not a mix of several.
If you pilot an Amoeba: perform movement and nutrition by flowing and extending pseudopods to creep along and to surround and engulf a drifting food particle (no mouth or stomach needed).

If you pilot a Euglena: perform movement and sensitivity by beating the flagellum to swim and using the eyespot to steer toward a patch of light (Euglena also makes food by photosynthesis rather than engulfing it).
If you pilot a Paramecium: perform movement by beating rows of cilia, and feed via the oral groove.

Perform excretion: pump the contractile vacuole (present in Amoeba, Euglena and Paramecium) to bail out excess water before the cell swells and bursts (waste such as carbon dioxide also diffuses out through the cell membrane).
Perform growth and reproduction: once energy/size is high enough, split the cell into two by binary fission.
Watch a survival indicator that falls whenever ANY one process is neglected, then state in your own words why the single cell has to do every job itself.
Afterwards, write one sentence answering: 'Which organs does this organism lack, and which parts of its single cell do those jobs instead?'
activities.insight: A unicellular organism is a complete, self-sufficient life: one cell performs every one of the seven life processes by itself, with its own organelles and adaptations doing the jobs that a multicellular body hands to specialised organs.

activities.title: Label the microbe and name each adaptation (naming layer)
steps: Study labelled diagrams of Amoeba, Euglena and/or Paramecium and identify the pseudopod (Amoeba), flagellum and eyespot (Euglena), cilia (Paramecium) and the contractile vacuole (all three).
For each adaptation, state the life process it carries out (e.g. flagellum → movement; contractile vacuole → excretion; eyespot → sensitivity).
Answer the prompt 'Are all single-celled organisms harmful?' and give an example of a harmless or helpful microbe (e.g. yeast, gut bacteria).

Reveal explanations after committing to an answer, e.g. selecting the flagellum shows 'whip-like tail for swimming'; selecting the contractile vacuole shows 'pumps out extra water so the cell doesn't burst.'
activities.insight: Each named structure in a single-celled organism performs a specific life process, different organisms use different adaptations for the same process, and most microbes are harmless or beneficial rather than disease-causing germs.

activities.title: Observe live pond microbes moving and feeding
steps: View pond water or a prepared Paramecium sample under a microscope, or watch a video of live microbes if a microscope is unavailable.
Describe what you see the organism actually doing: how it moves, how it changes direction, any feeding.
Match each observed behaviour to a life process and the structure likely responsible.
Optionally watch a free-swimming 3D or video Paramecium to appreciate cilia motion and the organism's scale in water.
activities.insight: Unicellular organisms are visibly alive — they move, respond to surroundings and feed — not merely static diagram labels.

activities.title: Compare unicellular self-sufficiency with multicellular division of labour
steps: Place a single-celled organism side by side with a specialised multicellular cell (e.g. a muscle cell or nerve cell).
Explain what the single cell must do that the specialised cell does not — and vice versa.
Answer: 'What can a multicellular organism do that a single-celled one can't, and why does having many cells help?'
State why multicellular organisms are not just 'bigger versions' of single cells.
activities.insight: Multicellular organisms share life's jobs among specialised cells (division of labour), which is a solution to a size/complexity problem; they are not simply enlarged single cells.

activities.title: Consolidation check: match structures, sort processes, and explain in role
steps: Match each microbe structure to the life process it performs.
Sort a set of features into the seven life processes.
Answer short questions contrasting unicellular and multicellular organisms.
Optionally take on the role 'I am an Amoeba — ask me how I survive' and explain in your own words how the organism eats, moves and avoids bursting.
activities.insight: Learners can independently name adaptations, map them to the correct life process, and articulate the unicellular-vs-multicellular contrast.

checkQuestion: An amoeba is just one single cell — no heart, no lungs, no legs. Can something made of only one cell really be fully alive: can it feed, move, get rid of waste and reproduce? Explain how a single cell manages all of that.
checkAnswer: Yes — a unicellular organism carries out all seven life processes within its one cell: it moves (an amoeba flows using pseudopodia), feeds (engulfs food), respires, excretes waste across its membrane, grows, reproduces by dividing, and senses its surroundings. It needs no organs because the single cell and its organelles do every job.
